prompt: On a given circle, six points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, and $F$ are chosen at random, independently and uniformly with respect to arc length. Determine the probability that the two triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ are disjoint, i.e., have no common points.

solutions.title: Only the circular order matters
solutions.body:
With probability $1$ the six points are distinct. Condition on the set of six positions; by symmetry every assignment of the labels $A,\dots,F$ to these positions is equally likely.

**When are the triangles disjoint?** Colour $A,B,C$ red and $D,E,F$ blue, and read the colours around the circle.
- If the three red points are consecutive (the reds form one arc, the blues the complementary arc), pick a point of the circle in each of the two gaps between the arcs; the chord through these two points separates the plane, with each triangle (the convex hull of points on one open arc) strictly on one side. So the triangles are disjoint.
- Otherwise the colours form at least four alternating blocks, so there are red points $R_1, R_2$ and blue points $B_1,B_2$ in the circular order $R_1, B_1, R_2, B_2$. Chords with alternating endpoints on a circle cross, so the side $R_1R_2$ (of the red triangle) meets $B_1B_2$ (of the blue one): the triangles intersect.

**Count.** The red labels occupy a uniformly random $3$-element subset of the $6$ positions; there are $\binom63 = 20$ such subsets, of which exactly $6$ are circularly consecutive. So the probability is $\frac{6}{20} = \frac{3}{10}$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac{3}{10}$.

prompt:
Prove that the roots of
$$x^5 + ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e = 0$$
cannot all be real if $2a^2 < 5b$.
answer: If all roots $x_i$ are real, Vieta gives $2a^2-5b = \tfrac12\sum_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^2 \ge 0$, i.e. $2a^2\ge 5b$.

solutions.title: Vieta and a sum of squares
solutions.body:
Suppose all five roots $x_1,\dots,x_5$ are real. By Vieta, $a = -\sum x_i$ and $b = \sum_{i<j}x_ix_j$. Then
$$a^2 = \sum x_i^2 + 2b,\qquad\text{so}\qquad 2a^2 - 5b = 2\sum x_i^2 - b.$$
On the other hand,
$$\sum_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)^2 = 4\sum x_i^2 - 2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j = 4\sum x_i^2 - 2b,$$
since each $x_i^2$ occurs in $4$ of the $10$ pairs. Therefore
$$2a^2 - 5b = \frac12\sum_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^2\ge 0.$$
So if $2a^2 < 5b$, the roots cannot all be real. ∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body: With real roots, $2b = (\sum x_i)^2 - \sum x_i^2 = a^2 - \sum x_i^2$, and by Cauchy–Schwarz $\sum x_i^2\ge\frac15\left(\sum x_i\right)^2 = \frac{a^2}5$. Hence $2b\le a^2 - \frac{a^2}{5} = \frac{4a^2}{5}$, i.e. $5b\le 2a^2$. ∎

prompt: Each set of a finite family of subsets of a line is a union of two closed intervals. Moreover, any three of the sets of the family have a point in common. Prove that there is a point which is common to at least half the sets of the family.
answer: Write $S_i = [a_i,b_i]\cup[c_i,d_i]$ with $b_i\le c_i$; then every set contains $\alpha=\max a_i$ or $\delta=\min d_i$ (a set missing both could not share a point with the sets attaining $\alpha$ and $\delta$), so one of these two points lies in at least half the sets.

solutions.title: Largest left end and smallest right end
solutions.body:
If the family has at most two sets the claim is trivial (any point of one set lies in at least half of them), so assume $n\ge3$ sets. Then any two sets also meet (add a third set and use the hypothesis).

Write $S_i = [a_i,b_i]\cup[c_i,d_i]$ with $a_i\le b_i\le c_i\le d_i$ (a single interval $[a_i,d_i]$ can be written as $[a_i,d_i]\cup[d_i,d_i]$). So $a_i = \min S_i$ and $d_i = \max S_i$. Let
$$\alpha = \max_i a_i = a_h,\qquad \delta = \min_i d_i = d_k.$$
Then $\alpha\in S_h$, every point of $S_h$ is $\ge\alpha$, and $\delta\in S_k$, every point of $S_k$ is $\le\delta$.

**Claim: every $S_i$ contains $\alpha$ or $\delta$.** Suppose $S_i$ contains neither (so $i\ne h$, $i\ne k$).
- Since $a_i\le\alpha$ and $\alpha\notin[a_i,b_i]$, we get $b_i<\alpha$. All points of $S_h$ are $\ge\alpha > b_i$, so $S_i\cap S_h\subseteq[c_i,d_i]$, and in fact $S_i\cap S_h\subseteq(b_i, d_i]$.
- Since $d_i\ge\delta$ and $\delta\notin[c_i,d_i]$, we get $c_i>\delta$. All points of $S_k$ are $\le\delta<c_i$, so $S_i\cap S_k\subseteq[a_i, c_i)$, i.e. $S_i \cap S_k \subseteq [a_i,b_i]$.

A point common to $S_i$, $S_h$, $S_k$ (if $h = k$, a point common to $S_i$ and $S_h$) would lie in $(b_i,d_i]\cap[a_i,b_i] = \varnothing$ — a contradiction.

**Conclusion.** Every set contains $\alpha$ or $\delta$, so the numbers of sets containing $\alpha$ and containing $\delta$ add up to at least $n$; one of them is at least $\frac n2$. ∎

prompt: Six segments $S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4, S_5,$ and $S_6$ are given in a plane. These are congruent to the edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, BD,$ and $CD$, respectively, of a tetrahedron $ABCD$. Show how to construct a segment congruent to the altitude of the tetrahedron from vertex $A$ with straight-edge and compasses.
answer: Draw face $BCD$; fold faces $ABC$ and $ABD$ into its plane (getting $A_1, A_2$); the perpendiculars from $A_1$ to $BC$ and from $A_2$ to $BD$ meet at the foot $H$ of the altitude; with $F$ the foot on $BC$, the altitude is the leg $\sqrt{A_1F^2-FH^2}$ of a right triangle.

solutions.title: Unfold two faces
solutions.body:
Ruler and compasses can transfer lengths, construct a triangle from three given sides, drop perpendiculars and erect perpendiculars, so all steps below are Euclidean constructions.

**Construction.**
1. Construct triangle $BCD$ with $BC = |S_4|$, $BD = |S_5|$, $CD = |S_6|$.
2. Construct $A_1$ with $A_1B = |S_1|$, $A_1C = |S_2|$ (intersect two circles), and $A_2$ with $A_2B = |S_1|$, $A_2D = |S_3|$.
3. Drop the perpendicular $\ell_1$ from $A_1$ to line $BC$, with foot $F$, and the perpendicular $\ell_2$ from $A_2$ to line $BD$. Let $H = \ell_1\cap\ell_2$.
4. Draw the circle with center $F$ through $A_1$ and erect the perpendicular to $\ell_1$ at $H$; let it meet the circle at $Z$. Then $HZ$ is the required segment.

**Proof.** Place the real tetrahedron with face $BCD$ equal to the constructed triangle, and let $H'$ be the orthogonal projection of $A$ onto plane $BCD$ and $F'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $BC$.

Since $BC\perp AF'$ and $BC\perp AH'$ (as $AH'$ is perpendicular to the whole plane), $BC$ is perpendicular to plane $AF'H'$, so $F'H'\perp BC$: the point $H'$ lies on the line in plane $BCD$ through $F'$ perpendicular to $BC$.

Rotating triangle $ABC$ about $BC$ into the plane $BCD$ sends $A$ to a point with distances $AB, AC$ from $B, C$, i.e. to $A_1$ or its mirror image in $BC$; in either case the foot of the perpendicular to $BC$ stays $F'$, and $A_1F'\perp BC$ with $A_1F' = AF'$. Hence $F = F'$ and $\ell_1$ is the line through $F$ perpendicular to $BC$, which contains $H'$. In the same way $\ell_2$ is the line through the foot on $BD$ perpendicular to $BD$, and it contains $H'$. As $BC\not\parallel BD$, the lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ are not parallel and meet in exactly one point, so $H = H'$.

Finally, triangle $AH'F$ has a right angle at $H'$, so
$$AH'^2 = AF^2 - FH^2 = A_1F^2 - FH^2 = FZ^2 - FH^2 = HZ^2,$$
because $FZ = FA_1$ and $FHZ$ is right-angled at $H$. (In particular $FH \le FA_1$, so $Z$ exists; if $H = F$, $Z$ is simply a point at distance $FA_1$ on the perpendicular.) So $HZ$ is congruent to the altitude from $A$. ∎

prompt: Consider an open interval of length $1/n$ on the real number line, where $n$ is a positive integer. Prove that the number of irreducible fractions $p/q$, with $1\le q\le n$, contained in the given interval is at most $(n+1)/2$.
answer: Two such fractions in the interval cannot have denominators $q$ and $kq$ (their difference would be $\ge \frac1{kq}\ge\frac1n$), so the denominators are distinct and no one divides another; grouping $1,\dots,n$ by odd part shows there are at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ of them.

solutions.title: Denominators form a divisibility antichain
solutions.body:
Let $I$ be the open interval and suppose $\frac pq\ne\frac{p'}{q'}$ are irreducible fractions in $I$ with $1\le q, q'\le n$ and $q' = kq$ for a positive integer $k$. Then
$$\left|\frac pq - \frac{p'}{kq}\right| = \frac{|kp - p'|}{kq}\ge\frac1{kq}\ge\frac1n,$$
because $kp - p'$ is a nonzero integer (the fractions are different numbers). But two points of an open interval of length $\frac1n$ are less than $\frac1n$ apart — contradiction.

Hence the fractions in $I$ have **distinct** denominators (the case $k=1$), and **no denominator divides another**.

**Bounding such a set of denominators.** Write each $m\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ as $m = 2^j u$ with $u$ odd. Two numbers with the same odd part $u$ are $2^ju$ and $2^{j'}u$, and the smaller divides the larger. So the denominators have pairwise different odd parts. The odd numbers in $\{1,\dots,n\}$ number $\lceil n/2\rceil\le\frac{n+1}2$.

Therefore $I$ contains at most $\frac{n+1}{2}$ such fractions. ∎
